nodes.title: Hybrid cloud connectivity: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Hybrid connectivity links on-premises networks to the cloud either over the public internet via encrypted VPN or over a dedicated private circuit. Exams expect you to compare the two, recognize each cloud's private-circuit product, and know how routes and redundancy are handled.

flashcards.front: Contrast site-to-site IPsec VPN with a dedicated private circuit.
flashcards.back: An IPsec VPN encrypts traffic over the public internet — fast to set up, low cost, but variable performance. A dedicated private circuit is a provisioned, private connection bypassing the internet for consistent bandwidth and lower latency.

flashcards.front: Name the dedicated private-circuit product for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
flashcards.back: AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute, and Google Cloud Interconnect — all provide a private, dedicated link from your network to the cloud provider instead of going over the internet.

flashcards.front: What is hub-and-spoke topology in hybrid networking?
flashcards.back: A central hub network holds shared connectivity and services (VPN/circuit, firewalls), and spoke networks connect to it rather than to each other — centralizing transit, security, and route control.

flashcards.front: How are routes exchanged and made highly available across these links?
flashcards.back: BGP dynamically advertises and learns routes between on-prem and the cloud gateway. Redundancy is built with paired/HA gateways and multiple tunnels or circuits so a single device or link failure does not drop connectivity.

questions.q: You need a site-to-site VPN connection into an Azure virtual network that survives the failure of a single Azure VPN gateway instance and also provides higher aggregate throughput. Which configuration should you use?
choices: Deploy the VPN gateway in active-active mode, which provisions two gateway instances each with its own public IP address
Deploy a single Basic SKU VPN gateway and rely on the Azure platform SLA to recover the instance
Create two separate VPN gateways in the GatewaySubnet of the same virtual network
Provision a route-based gateway in active-passive mode and add a second local network gateway
questions.explanation: Active-active mode provisions two gateway instances, each with its own public IP, so the on-premises device builds tunnels to both — surviving a single-instance failure and increasing aggregate throughput. The Basic SKU is always a single instance and supports neither active-active nor BGP. A virtual network can contain at most one VPN gateway, so two gateways in one GatewaySubnet is not possible. A second local network gateway describes another on-premises site; in active-passive only one gateway instance is active at a time.

questions.q: A company connects to Microsoft over an ExpressRoute circuit and must reach both Azure IaaS VMs inside virtual networks and Microsoft 365 plus public Azure PaaS endpoints over that same circuit. Which peering configuration is required?
choices: Azure private peering for the virtual networks and Microsoft peering for Microsoft 365 and public PaaS services

Azure private peering only, because it carries all Microsoft traffic — private peering reaches only IaaS workloads inside virtual networks; it cannot route to public PaaS endpoints or Microsoft 365, which require Microsoft peering to be separately enabled on the circuit
Microsoft peering only, because it supersedes private peering
Azure public peering for everything, because it was simply renamed to Microsoft peering
questions.explanation: An ExpressRoute circuit supports two routing domains: Azure private peering carries traffic to virtual networks (IaaS), and Microsoft peering carries traffic to Microsoft public services such as Microsoft 365 and public Azure PaaS endpoints. Reaching both kinds of destination requires enabling both peerings. Private peering alone cannot reach Microsoft 365; Microsoft peering alone cannot reach VNet VMs. Azure public peering is a deprecated legacy peering and is not equivalent to Microsoft peering.

questions.q: An organization has 30 branch offices and workloads in 6 Azure regions. It wants a Microsoft-managed hub-and-spoke topology where branches connect with site-to-site VPN and SD-WAN, and routing between hubs and spokes is handled automatically. Which Azure offering should it adopt?
choices: A self-managed hub virtual network in each region, peered together in a manually maintained mesh
An Azure Route Server deployed in every spoke virtual network
Azure Virtual WAN with a virtual hub in each region
A dedicated Azure VPN gateway deployed in every spoke virtual network
questions.explanation: Azure Virtual WAN provides Microsoft-managed virtual hubs that aggregate site-to-site VPN, point-to-site VPN, ExpressRoute, and SD-WAN connectivity, with automatic any-to-any routing between hubs and spokes. A manually meshed hub-and-spoke topology is exactly the operational burden Virtual WAN removes. Azure Route Server exchanges routes with network virtual appliances but does not provide a managed hub topology. A VPN gateway per spoke does not scale to 30 branches across 6 regions.

questions.q: A hub virtual network contains an Azure VPN gateway. Spoke virtual networks are peered to the hub and must reach on-premises networks through that single gateway without each spoke having its own gateway. Which peering settings achieve this?
choices: Enable 'Allow gateway transit' on both sides of every hub-to-spoke peering
On the hub side of the peering enable 'Allow gateway transit', and on the spoke side enable 'Use the remote virtual network's gateway'
On the hub side enable 'Use the remote virtual network's gateway', and on the spoke side enable 'Allow gateway transit'
Deploy a VPN gateway in every spoke and disable gateway transit on all peerings
questions.explanation: The virtual network that owns the gateway (the hub) must allow gateway transit on its side of the peering, and the virtual network that consumes it (each spoke) must select 'Use the remote virtual network's gateway' on its side. This lets spokes use the hub gateway for on-premises connectivity without their own gateways. Enabling transit on both sides, or reversing the two settings, does not establish the relationship, and a gateway per spoke defeats the centralized hub-and-spoke design.

questions.q: VMs spread across several spoke virtual networks must resolve each other by hostname automatically as the VMs are created and deleted, with no manual record maintenance. What should you configure?
choices: An Azure Private DNS zone linked to each virtual network with auto-registration enabled on those links
A public Azure DNS zone containing one manually created A record per VM

A custom DNS server VM in the hub running BIND with zone transfers to each spoke — BIND can resolve hostnames across virtual networks but requires manual zone maintenance; it does not support the automatic registration that creates and removes records as VMs appear and disappear
Only the Azure-provided default DNS resolver at 168.63.129.16 with no other configuration
questions.explanation: An Azure Private DNS zone linked to the virtual networks with the auto-registration option creates and removes DNS records automatically as VMs are provisioned and deprovisioned, and it resolves names across all linked VNets. A public DNS zone needs manual records and exposes names on the internet. A BIND server VM adds unnecessary operational overhead. The Azure-provided default DNS resolves hostnames only within a single virtual network, not across peered spokes.

questions.q: All traffic between two spoke virtual networks must be inspected by a network virtual appliance (NVA) located in the hub virtual network. What is the correct way to force spoke-to-spoke traffic through the NVA?
choices: Apply a network security group on each spoke subnet that allows only the NVA's IP address — an NSG can restrict which addresses are permitted to communicate, but it cannot redirect traffic through the virtual appliance; only a user-defined route can change the forwarding path
Enable 'Allow forwarded traffic' on the spoke-to-spoke virtual network peering
Configure BGP on the NVA and rely on Azure system routes to redirect traffic automatically
Associate a user-defined route table on each spoke subnet with a route to the other spoke's prefix using next hop type 'Virtual appliance' set to the NVA's private IP address
questions.explanation: A user-defined route on each spoke subnet, targeting the other spoke's address prefix with next hop type 'Virtual appliance' pointing at the NVA's private IP, forces that traffic through the appliance for inspection. Network security groups only allow or deny traffic; they cannot change its path. 'Allow forwarded traffic' permits transit traffic on a peering but does not steer it to the NVA. System routes by themselves send spoke-to-spoke traffic directly, so the explicit user-defined route is required.

questions.q: A security team needs centralized, stateful filtering of outbound traffic by fully qualified domain name (FQDN), threat intelligence-based filtering, and centralized logging for an entire hub-and-spoke network. Which service meets these requirements?
choices: Network security groups applied to every subnet in the topology
Application security groups referenced inside network security group rules
Azure Firewall deployed in the hub virtual network
Azure DDoS Protection enabled on the hub virtual network
questions.explanation: Azure Firewall is a managed, stateful, cloud-native network firewall that supports application rules with FQDN filtering, threat intelligence-based filtering, and centralized logging — making it the natural fit for a hub. Network security groups filter by IP address, port, protocol, and service tags but cannot filter arbitrary FQDNs or apply threat intelligence. Application security groups only group VM network interfaces for use within NSG rules. Azure DDoS Protection mitigates volumetric attacks and does not perform application-layer egress filtering.

questions.q: You must make an Azure SQL Database reachable from a virtual network using a private IP address inside that VNet, with no exposure of the database on the public internet. Which feature should you use?
choices: A service endpoint for Microsoft.Sql configured on the subnet — a service endpoint optimizes and secures the path to the SQL service's public IP but does not assign a private address inside the virtual network; the database public endpoint remains active
A private endpoint for the SQL Database that projects a private IP address into the subnet
The database's public endpoint restricted by the logical SQL server firewall to the VNet's outbound IP
An ExpressRoute Microsoft peering advertised toward the SQL Database
questions.explanation: A private endpoint creates a network interface with a private IP address from the subnet that maps to the PaaS resource, so traffic stays on the Microsoft backbone and the service needs no public exposure. A service endpoint still routes to the service's public IP — it secures and optimizes the path but leaves the public endpoint in place. A firewall-restricted public endpoint is still a public endpoint. ExpressRoute Microsoft peering provides reachability to public Microsoft services and does not project a private IP into a VNet.

nodes.title: Observability and monitoring: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Observability is metrics + logs + traces — the three pillars. You need all three to debug a production incident: metrics tell you something is wrong, logs tell you what happened, traces tell you where in the call graph the problem lives.

flashcards.front: Metrics vs logs vs traces — what does each tell you?
flashcards.back: Metrics: numeric time-series, cheap to store, perfect for dashboards and alerts ('p99 latency = 800 ms'). Logs: discrete events with context, expensive at scale, perfect for forensics. Traces: causally-linked spans showing a request's full path through services.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between an alert and a notification?
flashcards.back: An alert is a condition that fires when a metric crosses a threshold (CPU > 80% for 5 min). The notification is the resulting message (email, Slack, PagerDuty page). One alert can fan out to many notifications. Tuning alerts is harder than wiring notifications.

flashcards.front: What is an SLI / SLO / SLA?
flashcards.back: SLI (indicator): the metric you actually measure ('% of requests under 200 ms'). SLO (objective): the internal target ('99.9% of requests under 200 ms over 28 days'). SLA (agreement): the contractual promise to customers, usually weaker than the SLO so you have buffer.

Plain-text logs are unparseable at scale. Structured logs (JSON, with timestamp + level + service + request_id + key fields) are indexable, queryable, and join-able across services. Most platforms auto-extract fields from JSON without configuration.

questions.q: A backend pool of VMs behind an Azure Load Balancer must be resilient to the loss of an availability zone, and the VMs need a defined, explicit outbound internet connection. Which design is correct?
choices: A Basic SKU public Load Balancer relying on default outbound access — the Basic SKU is not zone-redundant and depends on implicit default outbound access that Microsoft is removing; it does not support the explicit outbound rule configuration needed for deterministic SNAT
An internal Standard SKU Load Balancer, because internal load balancers also provide outbound internet access
A Basic SKU internal Load Balancer combined with instance-level public IP addresses on each VM
A Standard SKU public Load Balancer paired with an outbound rule, or an attached NAT gateway, for explicit egress
questions.explanation: The Standard SKU Load Balancer is zone-aware and zone-redundant, and pairing it with an explicit outbound rule — or, preferably, a NAT gateway — provides deterministic SNAT egress. The Basic SKU is not zone-redundant, is being retired, and depends on implicit default outbound access that Microsoft is removing. An internal Load Balancer never provides outbound internet connectivity. A Basic internal Load Balancer does not meet the zone-resilience requirement.

questions.q: A web application needs Layer 7 load balancing with URL path-based routing (for example, /images and /api directed to different backend pools), TLS termination, and protection against common web exploits such as SQL injection. Which Azure service should you choose?
choices: Azure Load Balancer with health probes on each backend pool
Azure Traffic Manager configured with weighted routing
Azure Application Gateway on the Web Application Firewall (WAF) tier
Azure Front Door deployed without the Web Application Firewall enabled
questions.explanation: Application Gateway is a Layer 7 load balancer that provides URL path-based routing, multi-site hosting, and TLS termination, and its WAF tier protects against OWASP Top 10 exploits such as SQL injection. Azure Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 and cannot route by URL path. Traffic Manager is DNS-based global routing with no path awareness or web application firewall. Front Door without WAF satisfies the routing and TLS needs but leaves the application unprotected against the web exploits the requirement calls out.

questions.q: A global application is deployed across four Azure regions. You need to route each user to the lowest-latency healthy region, terminate TLS and cache static content at the network edge, and fail over automatically. Which service best meets all of these needs?
choices: Azure Traffic Manager using the performance routing method
Azure Front Door
An internal Standard SKU Load Balancer spanning all four regions
Azure DNS configured with weighted records for each region
questions.explanation: Azure Front Door is a global, edge-based Layer 7 entry point that performs latency-based routing to the closest healthy backend, terminates TLS at the edge, caches static content with its built-in content delivery capability, and fails over automatically. Traffic Manager is DNS-only: it can do performance routing and health-based failover but cannot terminate TLS or cache content. A Load Balancer is a regional service and internal load balancers have no internet-facing role. Weighted DNS records provide neither latency routing, TLS offload, nor caching.

questions.q: Operators report intermittent connectivity from a VM to an external endpoint. They need continuous, alertable monitoring of latency, packet loss, and reachability over time between the VM and that endpoint. Which Azure Network Watcher capability should you use?
choices: IP flow verify
Next hop
Effective security rules
Connection monitor
questions.explanation: Connection monitor provides continuous, ongoing monitoring of reachability, latency, and packet loss between a source such as a VM and a destination, recording metrics over time and supporting alerts. IP flow verify is a one-time check of whether a specific packet is permitted by network security group rules. Next hop returns the routing decision for a single packet. Effective security rules shows the aggregated NSG rules applied to a network interface — all three are point-in-time diagnostics rather than continuous monitoring.

questions.q: NSG rules reference dozens of individual VM IP addresses for the web, app and database tiers, and every scale-out means editing rules. How do you simplify this while keeping tier-to-tier restrictions?
choices: Application security groups: tag each NIC with its tier's ASG and write NSG rules between ASGs
Replace the NSG with an Azure Firewall policy that uses FQDN rules for each tier's VM hostnames
Move each tier into its own dedicated virtual network connected through global VNet peering
Assign static private IPs from reserved ranges per tier and reference the ranges in the rules
questions.explanation: ASGs make NSG rules membership-based: NICs join the web/app/db ASG and rules say 'allow app-asg → db-asg:1433' — new instances inherit the rules by joining the group, no rule edits. Reserved ranges still need manual discipline and rule sprawl; per-tier VNets add peering complexity for a filtering problem; Azure Firewall FQDN rules target outbound internet names, not east-west tiering.

questions.q: VMs in a subnet make thousands of short outbound connections to the same external service and start failing intermittently with SNAT port exhaustion behind a public load balancer. What is the recommended fix?
choices: Enable TCP reset on idle timeout on the load balancer so exhausted flows recycle faster under load
Associate a NAT gateway with the subnet so outbound flows use its scalable SNAT port pool
Add a second public IP to each VM's NIC so half the flows originate from a different address
Lower the load balancer health probe interval so unhealthy ports are reclaimed more quickly
questions.explanation: NAT Gateway is Azure's recommended outbound path: it provides up to 64k SNAT ports per attached public IP (scalable to 16 IPs), dynamic allocation, and takes precedence over load-balancer outbound SNAT for the subnet. TCP reset and probe tuning don't add ports; per-VM public IPs remove SNAT but expose every VM directly — the wrong trade.

questions.q: An ExpressRoute circuit must carry traffic to the company's own VNets AND to Microsoft 365 endpoints. Which peering configuration is correct?
choices: Public peering for the VNets and private peering for Microsoft 365, with route filters on both paths
Private peering alone, since Microsoft 365 endpoints resolve to private addresses over ExpressRoute
Private peering for the VNets and Microsoft peering (with route filters) for Microsoft 365
Two separate circuits, because a single ExpressRoute circuit supports only one peering type at a time
questions.explanation: Private peering extends your network to your VNets; Microsoft peering carries traffic to Microsoft public services (Microsoft 365, Azure PaaS public endpoints), with route filters selecting which service prefixes you receive. One circuit supports both peerings simultaneously; 'public peering' is retired; Microsoft 365 endpoints remain public addresses even over ExpressRoute.

questions.q: Fifteen developers working from home need individual encrypted access to VMs in a VNet, authenticated with Microsoft Entra ID, without installing a branch VPN device anywhere. What do you deploy?
choices: A site-to-site VPN from each developer's home router to the VNet's gateway subnet
Point-to-site VPN on the virtual network gateway with Microsoft Entra authentication
ExpressRoute Direct with a partner exchange port reserved for the development team
VNet service endpoints configured for the Microsoft.Compute resource provider
questions.explanation: Point-to-site VPN is per-device: each developer runs the Azure VPN Client, authenticates with Entra ID, and gets an encrypted tunnel into the VNet — no on-premises hardware. Site-to-site assumes a VPN device per site (home routers ×15 is the wrong model); ExpressRoute is dedicated circuit infrastructure; service endpoints connect subnets to PaaS services, not users to VNets.

nodes.title: DNS: Key Ideas
nodes.content: DNS turns names into addresses. Most outages traced to 'is it DNS?' get answered 'yes'. The exam tests record types, recursion vs iteration, TTL behavior, and how DNSSEC works.

flashcards.front: What do A, AAAA, CNAME, and MX records do?
flashcards.back: A: name → IPv4 address. AAAA: name → IPv6 address. CNAME: name → another name (an alias; cannot coexist with other records at the same name). MX: name → mail server with priority. TXT: arbitrary key-value (SPF, DKIM, domain ownership proofs). Memorize at least these five.

flashcards.front: Recursive vs authoritative resolver — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: Authoritative: the server that owns the zone — when you ask 'what's the A record for example.com?' it answers definitively. Recursive: the client-side resolver (your ISP's, 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8) that walks the DNS hierarchy on your behalf, asking root → TLD → authoritative. Your laptop talks to a recursive resolver; the resolver talks to authoritatives.

Tells caching resolvers how long to keep a record. Low TTL (60s) = fast failover when you change records, but more DNS queries. High TTL (24h) = fewer queries, but a config change takes a day to propagate. Drop TTL to 60s a few hours BEFORE a planned migration; restore high TTL after.

flashcards.front: DNSSEC — what attack does it prevent?
flashcards.back: Cache poisoning: attacker injects fake records into a recursive resolver. DNSSEC signs records with the zone's private key; resolvers validate the signature against the DNS-published public key. If the signature doesn't match, the record is rejected. Adds CPU and complexity; most resolvers still don't strictly validate, but it's slowly winning.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a service endpoint and a private endpoint for reaching an Azure Storage account from a VNet?
choices: Service endpoints require a DNS zone per service, while private endpoints work without any DNS changes
Service endpoints encrypt the traffic, while private endpoints rely on the application layer for encryption
Private endpoints are free of charge, while service endpoints are billed per gigabyte processed
A service endpoint optimizes the route to the service's PUBLIC endpoint; a private endpoint gives the service a PRIVATE IP inside your VNet
questions.explanation: Service endpoints keep traffic on the Azure backbone toward the service's public address and identify your subnet to its firewall; the service never enters your address space. A private endpoint injects a NIC with a private IP from your VNet, reachable over VPN/ExpressRoute and from peered networks — which is why it needs private DNS zones, costs per-hour/per-GB, and is the choice for full network isolation.

questions.q: Security policy forbids public IP addresses on any IaaS VM, yet administrators need browser-based RDP and SSH to VMs across several VNets. Which service satisfies this?
choices: Azure Bastion (Standard or higher) deployed in a hub VNet reachable from the spoke VNets
Just-in-time VM access in Defender for Cloud opening management ports on request for approved sources
An internal load balancer with inbound NAT rules mapping high ports to each VM's RDP port
Network security group rules restricting 3389 and 22 to the administrators' home IP ranges
questions.explanation: Bastion provides TLS-wrapped RDP/SSH through the portal (or native client) directly to private IPs — VMs need no public address, and with Standard SKU + IP-based connection it reaches peered VNets from a hub deployment. JIT and NSG scoping still presuppose a public path to the VM; an internal LB with NAT rules is only reachable from inside the network anyway and just relocates the problem.

questions.q: On-premises clients must resolve names in an Azure Private DNS zone (privatelink.database.windows.net) to reach private endpoints. Conditional forwarders cannot target the 168.63.129.16 resolver across VPN. What should you deploy?
choices: A secondary copy of the private zone hosted on the on-premises DNS servers with zone transfers
Azure DNS Private Resolver with an inbound endpoint that on-premises DNS servers forward to
Custom DNS settings on every on-premises client pointing directly at the Azure-provided resolver
A public DNS zone with the same records, so resolution succeeds from any network location
questions.explanation: DNS Private Resolver's inbound endpoint exposes a routable private IP inside the VNet that on-premises servers can conditionally forward to; queries then resolve against linked private zones. 168.63.129.16 is link-local and unreachable over VPN/ExpressRoute (whether forwarded from servers or set on clients); private zones don't support transfers out; publishing private endpoint IPs in public DNS leaks topology and breaks the privacy model.

questions.q: The security team asks which on-premises subnets have been connecting to which Azure VMs over the past month, with traffic volumes, visualized geographically. Which capability answers this?
choices: Connection troubleshoot in Network Watcher run against each VM pair the team cares about
Effective security rules view exported weekly for every network interface in the subscription
NSG flow logs analyzed with Traffic Analytics
Azure Monitor metrics on each NIC summed across the month with a workbook visualization
questions.explanation: Flow logs record allowed/denied flows per NSG (source, destination, port, bytes); Traffic Analytics aggregates them in Log Analytics into traffic patterns, talking-pairs, and geo-mapped visualizations over time — exactly the retrospective question asked. Connection troubleshoot and effective rules are point-in-time diagnostics; NIC metrics give byte counters with no flow-level who-to-whom detail.

questions.q: A global HTTP application needs TLS termination at Microsoft's edge, anycast-based instant failover between regional backends, URL-path routing, and an integrated WAF. Which service is designed for this combination?
choices: Traffic Manager with performance routing fronting regional application gateways in each geography
Azure Front Door (Standard/Premium)
A cross-region load balancer distributing layer-4 flows to regional public load balancers
Application Gateway v2 instances deployed per region behind a round-robin DNS record set
questions.explanation: Front Door is the global layer-7 entry point: anycast edge POPs terminate TLS close to users, route on paths/headers, fail over near-instantly (no DNS TTL wait), and Premium integrates the WAF. Traffic Manager is DNS-based — failover waits on TTLs and it can't terminate TLS or route paths; cross-region LB is layer 4; per-region gateways behind DNS round-robin reinvent Traffic Manager poorly.

questions.q: After a volumetric attack against a public-facing workload, the business wants tuned, telemetry-backed DDoS mitigation on its public IPs, cost protection guarantees, and access to a rapid-response team. What do you enable?
choices: Azure DDoS Network Protection on the virtual network hosting the public IP addresses
The default infrastructure-level DDoS protection that Azure applies to every public IP for free
A WAF policy in prevention mode attached to the application gateway fronting the workload
Azure Firewall Premium with IDPS signatures set to alert-and-deny for inbound traffic flows
questions.explanation: DDoS Network Protection (the paid tier) adds adaptive, per-resource tuned mitigation, attack telemetry and diagnostics, the DDoS Rapid Response team, and cost protection credits — the asks in the scenario. The free infrastructure protection is untuned and offers none of those guarantees; WAF stops layer-7 application attacks, not volumetric floods; Firewall IDPS inspects permitted flows rather than absorbing volumetric attacks.
